speechtext:
Earned income. Therefoie there is no finer security existing in Canada 

for loans made to veterans employed by the big corporations in my constituency who desire to build houses and make their permanent residence there. Owing to the present regulations many of these veterans have been denied that opportunity. Veterans generally, and the Legion in my constituency, are very dissatisfied with the, shall I say, production today under the terms of the Veterans Land Act, particularly with regard to the development of possibilities for small holdings.
In that connection I want to read a resolution that I received just a few days ago from the zone council of the Canadian Legion in my constituency, endorsed by every branch present:
Whereas we appreciate the value of the present settlement under the small holding section of the Veterans Land1 Act;
And whereas, owing to the rapid industrial development in west Kootenay, and subsequent demand for small holdings;
And whereas, the Kootenay climate, soil, rainfall, and topography, are different to the coast, Okanagan, and northern British Columbia;
And whereas, the present system of administration from Kelowna causes very serious delay in servicing applications;
And whereas, many potential sites are undeveloped, needing only a water system installed;
And whereas, a smaller acreage than the present three acres would be more practical in some areas.
Therefore be it resolved:
(1)	That the regional office be re-established at Nelson, B.C., for east and west Kootenay.
(2)	That a survey be made of potential developments, sub-divisions, and water system development where these would make additional land available.
(3)	That the acreage required for a small holding be reduced to suit the area.
That resolution was drafted after serious consideration of the whole situation by a special committee appointed to deal with it-not just a few men gathered together to air their grievances, without consideration of all the facts. These were men who were studying the question of local conditions and the needs of veterans concerned.
I point to that as one illustration of the need for a review of the Veterans Land Act, with a view to increasing the basic grant and changing the regulations in so far as the acreage of small holdings is concerned.
I wish the committee had been empowered and instructed to deal with the Legion's request for educational opportunities for dependent children. However, I shall not say any more about that at the present time, I do want to deal with one more question that has been brought to my attention in recent months, when I have come across many cases of older veterans who are not satisfactorily served by the legislation or who wish to continue working because they have

obligations and responsibilities that cannot be met by accepting the war veterans allowance, or things of that kind.
The question of the employment of older veterans is a very serious one, and one which in my opinion should have been referred to the committee. Manpower requirements in Canada at the present time demand that we use the services of every person who is willing and able to work. I understand that the Department of Labour has a branch in which there are officials endeavouring to find employment, particularly for older people, including veterans. It would include, for instance, the age group between fifty and sixty-five.
The government of this country is spending money in that connection. It has in its employ people who are paying particular attention to that problem. When it comes to the civil service, we find that, in connection with the reductions proposed, the policy of the government is to pay particular attention to the older civil servants, to have regard for their needs and, if they have to be displaced, to find employment for them. The Department of Veterans Affairs has a special branch which has been trying to persuade employers to employ a greater number of veterans between the ages of fifty and sixty-five. These are older veterans who are willing and anxious to work.
What do we find? I shall take time to give only two illustrations. Right in this building there is an older veteran who has been employed for twenty-two years as a messenger. He had four years' service in the 72nd battalion, and served in the first world war in Canada, England, France and Belgium. His present age is seventy. This man is vigorous, active and anxious to work. He is retired on a superannuation allowance of $48 a month, and draws a disability of $17 a month, making a total income of $65 a month.
Out of that $65 he has to maintain his wife, who is ill, which costs him $35 a month. That leaves the veteran in question with a balance of $30 on which he must live. Here is a veteran, fit and anxious to work, but who cannot live on $30 a month. He cannot receive the war veterans allowance in view of the income he receives. That man has been turned out of this building, although he is quite capable of carrying on as a messenger and doing the work he would be required to do. He is tramping the streets of Ottawa looking for a job, at a time when in Canada we need manpower.
I bring that to the attention of the minister and the house. Then I would turn to a case in my own constituency. As the result of 80709-105
Veterans Affairs-Special Committee instructions given recently to all departments, the Department of Veterans Affairs, in common with other government departments, had to lower its staff. Throughout the country, wherever it was considered possible, there have been reductions in staff.
In the Kootenays we have had three field men representing the Veterans Land Act administration. They have been covering an area in which there are about 80,000 people. In the office at Nelson there were three excellent and capable veterans who had been servicing the whole area. The question of economy has arisen and, in its wisdom, the Veterans Land Act administration has decided that one of the three must go. With that in mind they have chosen the oldest veteran, a veteran of two world wars, and the senior man from point of service in the interior of British Columbia. He is a man with long residence in that interior section and one who has had excellent relations with the veterans he has served through the years. This man is well liked by the veterans; he has been a most efficient official, and has done a good job for the Veterans Land Act administration. The department has paid tribute to his ability.
Here we have the Department of Veterans Affairs urging employers to retain the services of older men, while at the same time the Veterans Land Act administration in this instance disposes of its oldest and most experienced man. They put him out at an age when it is most difficult for him to get back into civilian life or to find another job.
This situation is so unjust and is so in opposition to the governments major policy, and the policy of the veterans affairs administration, that every branch of the Legion in my constituency has protested to the director of the Veterans Land Act administration. They have also sent letters and telegrams to me. The veterans in my constituency are deeply concerned about this situation, because it seems so much in contradiction to the announced policy of the government.
In my view if the Veterans Land Act is reviewed, if some of its terms are changed and if the regulations were changed so as to lower the acreage for small holdings, the three men could not do all the work required in the Kootenays to provide small holdings and farms for the veterans requiring them. In the district surrounding Nelson and Trail, in that new mine being developed by the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company at Riondel, all that is needed is a push in order to have a big development at all points. First of all there would have to be a change
1638	HOUSE OF
Veterans Affairs-Special Committee in the regulations, and then a little more push, and I am sure the three men we have there could do the job.
This older veteran has been dismissed. First of all he was asked to tender his resignation, but after his long service with the department he refused to do so. Finally he received a curt notice of dismissal from the office at Vancouver.
The result is that we are left with two men to cover the whole of the area of the Kootenays, with a total population of 80,000, and with the greatest demand for small holdings of any place in Canada, having in mind the population and the circumstances. The department has said that they will do what they can to see if they can get him a job somewhere else. He is in that age group where it is most difficult to get a job.
The Nelson office has been closed except that it is to be open on Saturdays. This means that in the whole area there will be a Veterans Land Act administration office open only for a few hours a week during which time veterans will be able to make applications and so on. This creates a most inconvenient situation because many veterans have to come 50, 60 or even 150 miles in order to see the person in charge of the office. These shorter hours will simply mean greater expense for the veterans who will have to fit their own time to the hours when the office is open.
I greatly appreciate the co-operation given by officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs. As I have said before, the minister, the parliamentary assistant and the officials have been most co-operative with members of the house and have done an excellent job. I am particularly concerned about the employment of older veterans, and particularly about the dismissal of this older veteran from the Nelson office of the Veterans Land Act administration. There is a great demand for small holdings in my district which is not being met today. I hope the minister, the parliamentary assistant and the officials concerned will really review that situation to see if something cannot be done to correct it. I know in saying this I have the unanimous support of every Legion branch in my constituency.
In conclusion, may I say that I look forward again to serving on this committee with comrades representing all the other parties. I trust 'that when the findings of the committee are presented to this house there will follow amendments to the legislation that will prove that the members of the veterans affairs committee have once again had an opportunity to serve the veterans of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, earlier in the debate I made a statement to the effect that the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) had stated in the house when he was Minister of Veterans Affairs that he would like to see the war veterans allowance in each province brought up to the amount of the old age pension paid in that province. The minister denied that he had made any such statement and I was eventually compelled to withdraw. I have here Hansard of Tuesday, June 6, 1950. At that time I had raised this very question, I believe on the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs, and the minister is reported on page 3294 as having said:
When social security for the aged is worked out on behalf of all our people, then, whether it is five years or ten years, whatever it might be, I hope that the amount of the war veterans allowance going to the veteran in each of the provinces, in that period between 60 and 70 we shall say, will be the same as it would be for all the people after the age of 70. In other words, in my own province-
That is New Brunswick.
-at the present time the war veterans allowance between 60 and 70 is almost exactly the same as the old age pension for the rest of the people from 70 until death. In my hon. friend's province,-
That would be British Columbia.
-for 75 per cent of the recipients, the war veterans allowance has been augmented to bring it up to $50 per month as a sort of cost of living bonus.
Then follow the words to which I have particular reference:
I should like to see the time when the veterans of the various provinces will receive the same as the residents of those provinces are receiving under the old age pension. Now, it is going to take a lot of planning to work that out, but in reality that is the real reason why I would rather see hardship overcome during these two years by this patchwork method, if you will, rather than by making an over-all increase from the eastern border of Saskatchewan to Newfoundland inclusive, which would bring the war veterans allowance, from 60 until death, ten dollars higher than the old age pension from 70 until death for the rest of the population.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention in closing the debate on this resolution to touch on all the points that have been raised by hon. members. I think it will be agreed that most of those matters will be dealt with more adequately, either in committee or when other legislation or the estimates are before the house.
Reference has been made to the necessity of having a standing committee on veterans affairs. If one goes over the history of veterans legislation enacted during the last 25 or 30 years it will be found that a veterans affairs committee has been constituted each time major changes have been made in the legislation, or when new legislation was introduced.
Reference has also been made during this debate to the terms of reference of the committee. I cannot subscribe to the statement that has been made that in the past the terms of reference setting up similar committees have always been much wider. In fact that is the case for the committees set up in 1945 and 1946. But in 1948 the terms of reference for the committee set up then were more restricted than in 1945 and 1946. My hon. friend who quoted the terms of reference in 1948 will notice that in that year there was no mention of the War Veterans Allowance Act. It will be found that in the past committees have been set up to consider only one specific act or amendment.
I think the house will agree that the years 1945 and 1946 were different. At that time we were bringing before the committee all the legislation which had been created during the war and immediately following the war in the form of orders in council. If I am not mistaken, I believe there were practically eighty-nine orders in council which were placed on the table of the committee to be considered, along with legislation which had been implemented since 1921.
That is not the case now. We are making the terms of reference wide enough to cover all legislation which is considered necessary at this time as well as any other legislation which the government may find it necessary to introduce before the end of this session.

I should like to touch upon one other point, the interpretation given by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) to the terms of reference. That is not the case, as one can readily see by reading the terms of reference. The hon. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, yesterday I announced that I would move to go into supply and call four different departments. I understand that some members wish to speak and I dare not make that motion at the present time. It would have no object and it would give them a chance to air their grievances for only two or three minutes. If I have the unanimous consent of the house that there will be no discussion I would move to go into supply. If there is not unanimous consent-

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Go ahead and move it.
